summary: This excerpt from Kate Douglas Wiggin's novel Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm (labelled 'Book 11 — part 23' in the note) describes the bare, uncomfortable village schoolroom where Rebecca studies under teacher Miss Dearborn. It explains how the class is informally divided, how Rebecca is hard to classify, and how she moves through history and other subjects at her own pace. It closes by introducing Samuel Simpson, nicknamed Seesaw, a pale, indecisive boy who is fascinated by Rebecca despite her snubs.
one_line: A passage from a novel describing a rural schoolroom, Rebecca's uneven progress through lessons, and the indecisive boy Seesaw Simpson who admires her.
key_facts: The schoolroom had twenty scholars in Rebecca's time.
The villages along the river spent so much on repairing and rebuilding bridges that they had to be very economical with school privileges.

The room contained a teacher's desk and chair on a platform, an uncouth stove blackened at most once a year, a map of the United States, two black-boards, and a ten-quart tin pail of water with a long-handled dipper.
The seats were higher at the back of the room, where the more advanced and longer-legged pupils sat, nearer the windows and farther from the teacher.
Miss Dearborn gave up trying to classify Rebecca altogether after a fortnight.
Rebecca read with Dick Carter and Living Perkins, who were preparing for the academy.
Rebecca recited arithmetic with lisping little Thuthan Thimpthon and geography with Emma Jane Perkins.
Rebecca studied grammar after school hours with Miss Dearborn alone.
At first Rebecca made only a poor hand at composition because the labor of writing and spelling, along with punctuation and capitals, interfered with expressing her ideas.
Rebecca took history with Alice Robinson's class, which was studying the Revolution, though Rebecca was told to begin with the discovery of America.
Rebecca mastered the course of events up to the Revolution in a week and reached Yorktown in ten days.
Rebecca deliberately held herself back to avoid reciting with the oldest Simpson boy.
Samuel Simpson was called Seesaw because of his difficulty in making up his mind.
Seesaw was pale, flaxen haired, blue eyed, round shouldered, and stammered when nervous.
Despite Rebecca snubbing him to the verge of madness, Seesaw could never keep his eyes away from her.
